channel.title: Ajahn Paññāvaddho Quotes
channel.description: Dhamma quotes by Ajaan Paññāvaddho, updated every 6 hours

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: There are valuable lessons in the stories of Christian monastics. The value is in the qualities of the people involved. Some of them…
item.description:
Lessons from Non-Buddhist Spiritual Practitioners

There are valuable lessons in the stories of Christian monastics. The value is in the qualities of the people involved. Some of them had remarkably good qualities. One monk, a Russian orthodox, went to a quiet place in the forest to live, and after a time people came and found him. Before long they started to build a monastery there. That’s when he realized he should go to another place. So he went to another quiet place, and eventually the same thing happened again. So he moved again. In other words, the world was trying to catch him all the time. But he refused to be caught by it. It’s reminiscent of the simile of the log. Buddha saw a log of wood floating down the Ganges and he told his disciples that the log would eventually reach the ocean, provided it didn’t get snagged up by various obstacles.

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Anger seldom arises on its own. Like a forest fire that spreads through various types of undergrowth, anger builds and intensifies through the…
item.description:
The Relationship Between Aversion, Mental States, and the Force of Anger

"Anger seldom arises on its own. Like a forest fire that spreads through various types of undergrowth, anger builds and intensifies through the interplay of several other unwholesome mental states. Emotions like aversion, ill will, hatred, and resentment work together, each supporting and strengthening the others to produce a continuous cycle of suffering. Feelings of aversion are often the first stirrings of trouble in the mind. Aversion is experienced as an instinctive turning away from what we find unpleasant or threatening. When we encounter a person or situation that challenges our well-being or sense of security, aversion's immediate rejection creates favorable conditions for more deeply rooted negative states to develop. Rather than observing this discomfort mindfully and then letting it go, we hold on to it, allowing the negativity to open a door to more powerful defilements. Anger, in contrast, is an energetic and confrontational emotion that moves towards the perceived cause of its discomfort. While aversion recoils from contact, anger pushes forward to meet it head-on. Anger arises when we feel threatened or when we believe our boundaries have been encroached upon. It contains within it the desire to change or even eliminate the source of our displeasure. This is why the Buddha included anger among the dangers to our spiritual progress, because it carries such forceful energy."

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "So it is important to realize that no matter what your situation is you can always practice meditation. That’s not to say that…
item.description:
Understanding the Union of Citta and Kilesas

"So it is important to realize that no matter what your situation is you can always practice meditation. That’s not to say that it is always easy; it’s not. But it is only difficult because of the kilesas, which shows that we should look at the kilesas to understand what they are. In the final analysis, the kilesas are actually oneself – oneself as one is at this moment. But it is only after you have been practicing for a long time that you can come to separate your essential nature from the kilesas. Up to that point, you and the kilesas are one and the same because they are infused into the citta like dye in water. When they are mixed together, you cannot separate out the dye from the water, yet they are not the same. It’s the same with the citta. When the citta is colored by the kilesas, the whole of it is discolored in the same way. That defiling discoloration constantly leads you in the wrong direction, which is what makes the practice so difficult. If you can learn to see the kilesas and understand how bad they are, you can begin to overcome them."

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Added to that limitation, science cannot investigate that which lies beyond the realm of physical phenomena. In the same way that a ruler…
item.description:
The Failure of Science to Measure Internal Realities

"Added to that limitation, science cannot investigate that which lies beyond the realm of physical phenomena. In the same way that a ruler cannot measure weight and scales cannot measure length, can science measure "metta", for example? Can it quantify the peace that comes from "samadhi"? Can it put the Four Noble Truths under a microscope? The very suggestion shows its limitations, for these factors are among the most fundamental and important aspects of human existence, as well as the path to liberation. Many modern scientists... have fallen into what the Lord Buddha would recognize as a form of wrong view. They have become so enamored with the success gained by the scientific method in its own sphere that they have convinced themselves it is the only valid way of knowing anything. This attitude is rather like a carpenter becoming so skilled with his hammer that he begins to think every problem can be solved by hammering. Scientists will say, 'Give us enough time and funding, and we will reduce consciousness, morality, and the meaning of life itself to entirely physical processes in the brain.' Many such people become lost in intellectual mazes of scientific and philosophical speculation while their fundamental moral development remains neglected.",

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "When you talk of an Arahant being alive, you must think it possible for the Arahant to be dead, as well. But this…
item.description:
The Nature of the Arahant as a Pure Citta

"When you talk of an Arahant being alive, you must think it possible for the Arahant to be dead, as well. But this isn’t the case. Nibbāna is not in the realm of life and death. The Arahant is not the five khandhas, which are subject to birth and decay. The Arahant is a pure citta, and the pure citta never dies. So, in that sense, we can say that the Arahants are all there all the time. But we cannot sense them in any way. That doesn’t mean that they cannot help us, maybe they can. But we cannot understand that type of help they give because it is not the same type of help one person gives to another."

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Instinctively, we harbor a lot of anxiety about sickness, aging, and death—anxiety that saps our vitality as we expend so much energy denying…
item.description:
Transforming Anxiety into Spiritual Urgency

"Instinctively, we harbor a lot of anxiety about sickness, aging, and death—anxiety that saps our vitality as we expend so much energy denying those inescapable truths. Ironically, everyone knows they are going to die, but they act as though they don't believe it. What would change if they truly accepted that this breath might be their last—not just rationally, but deeply in their hearts? Would they waste time on petty grievances or postpone their spiritual practice for some imagined future that might never arrive? If they honestly believed in their own death, they would live their lives differently. Awareness of the inevitability of death means always being prepared to face that moment calmly and mindfully. When people accept that they can die at any time, the activities they normally waste their time on will appear trivial. They'll naturally become more involved in the quality of the life they are living, and their priorities are bound to shift as they make more room in their lives for spiritual pursuits. The things that previously seemed so important—the promotions, the social status, the material acquisitions—these begin to look rather hollow."

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Really speaking, your present life situation is where you are, and in that situation you have to make do with what you have.…
item.description:
Using Body Contemplation to Overcome Difficulties

"Really speaking, your present life situation is where you are, and in that situation you have to make do with what you have. So you have to find a way to practice in that situation, which takes advantage of your strengths while at the same time diminishing your weaknesses. When you find that it is frustrating and difficult, you should realize that sometimes life is difficult. You have to be patient and still try to practice the Dhamma unperturbed as far as possible by the difficulties. You can look and question yourself, who is the one inside that is troubled by the situation. Look at hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth and skin, flesh, blood, bones and so on, and question: where in that mess does the problem lie? When you keep your mind focused on by the contemplation, Dhamma comes to the fore and difficulties seem less important. If you keep your mind focused on what you are doing in the present moment, there is no time for frustration and difficulties. You are practicing the way, and that’s enough to bring satisfaction into a difficult situation. When you keep your mind focused in the present, distracting thoughts don’t come up. When distracting thoughts don’t come up, the mind remains well concentrated."

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: So the body is necessary, and it’s valuable. But we also have to come to realize that this body is not the nice,…
item.description:
The Burdensome Nature of the Body

So the body is necessary, and it’s valuable. But we also have to come to realize that this body is not the nice, pleasant thing that most people think of it as. It’s a burdensome thing. We have to carry it about all over the place and that’s tiresome. If we use it for any length of time we get exhausted. The body is unpleasant in all sorts of ways. In the hot weather it sweats and feels uncomfortable. The body gives us a lot of trouble all the time. It’s often unwell, feels sick, perhaps you have a slight headache or bodily aches and pains, feeling tension, not feeling completely at ease. It’s all dukkha, the whole lot. The body brings us a lot of dukkha. If we can come to realize that this body is not me, then we realize that we have to have the patience to put up with it.

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: Because we have learnt to view the world in a certain way without questioning that view, we cannot see what’s wrong. The perception…
item.description:
Overcoming Childhood Conditioning and Emotional Guilt

Because we have learnt to view the world in a certain way without questioning that view, we cannot see what’s wrong. The perception of the world that we learnt at a young age went in very deep and has stuck there. When we became adults, we still retained that childhood view. In other words, the child is still there. And all the attitudes, ideas, ways of thinking, beliefs and so on coming from childhood are riddled with delusion. The emotional residue left over from many people’s childhood is guilt. The surest way to deal with guilt is to first accept it. Most people instinctively try to resist their guilt, saying: “I’m not guilty!”. If you turn and say: “Alright, I accept the guilt. I am guilty!” you probably won’t even know what you are guilty of. You may find that the whole sequence starts to break up. The important point is to accept it. You know that the guilt is there because you can feel it. It’s a valid emotion. But it is the ‘I’ that’s guilty, the ‘self’. And that is a delusion to start with.

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Ignorance or avijjā is the root of the problem and its servants spread out from it. These are the so called kilesas –…
item.description:
The Nature of the Kilesas and the Inward Battle

"Ignorance or avijjā is the root of the problem and its servants spread out from it. These are the so called kilesas – or defilements, which in their root form consist of greed, hate, and delusion. But they spread out from these three into a whole range of derived qualities including anxiety, worry, slothfulness, laziness, jealousy, stinginess, selfishness, arrogance and so on. The kilesas are always waiting, ready to adapt any of theses modes to our thoughts, emotions and actions. But we do not realise that they are there and we do not understand what a burden they are. These are what leads us out into the world, and they act almost like demons. When we are doing meditation practice, the more success we gain in the practice the more these kilesas will resist and try to stop us. The reason for this is that these kilesas are in the heart, and Dhamma, the way of truth, is also in the heart. So there is a battle going on. Because the kilesas are situated in the heart they try to use the power of the human mind to force it to go out in the wrong direction. And by using the power of the mind the kilesas are very subtle and they are very clever in their ways of doing this. They act just like demons."
